topic.title: Arrays & Hashing
topic.summary: The most common interview topic: hash maps and sets for O(1) lookups, frequency counting, prefix sums and Kadane — the tools that turn O(n²) brute force into one pass.
topic.overview:
Most first-round coding questions are **array problems with an O(n²) brute force and an O(n) solution that uses a hash map, a set, or a running value**. Interviewers want to see you:

- state the brute force and its complexity first, then **name the repeated work** you can remove;
- reach for a **hash map or set** when you need "have I seen X?" or "how many times?" in O(1);
- build **prefix sums / prefix products** when the question is about ranges or "everything except me";
- keep a **running best** (Kadane) when the answer is the best contiguous subarray;
- explain *why* the hash map is O(1) on average and when it degrades.

**Core patterns in this topic**
1. Complement lookup (Two Sum): store what you have seen, look up what you need.
2. Frequency counting (anagrams, top-k): count, then compare or bucket the counts.
3. Canonical key (group anagrams): map every item to a key shared by its group.
4. Set membership with run starts (longest consecutive sequence).
5. Prefix sum + hash map (subarray sum equals k).
6. Prefix × suffix (product except self) and Kadane (maximum subarray).
7. One set per group (valid sudoku) and length-prefix encoding (encode and decode strings).
8. In-place matrix work: transpose + reverse (rotate image), shrinking boundaries (spiral matrix), markers in row 0 and column 0 (set matrix zeroes).

**How to study:** solve each question yourself first with a 20-minute timer, then step through the visual. Do how-hash-map-works right after the hash-map questions — it is the follow-up to almost all of them. For the matrix problems, trace a non-square matrix by hand: that is where the index bugs hide.

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.prompt:
You get an integer array `nums` and an integer `target`. Find the **two different positions** whose values add up to `target` and return their indices as `[i, j]` with `i < j`.

The input always has exactly one such pair, and an element cannot be paired with itself.

examples.explanation: Two equal values at different indices are allowed.

hints: The brute force tries every pair. Which work is repeated?
If the current number is x, its partner must be exactly target − x.
Keep a map from value to index of everything you have passed; look up target − x before you insert x.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every pair (i, j) with i < j and return the first that sums to target.

approaches.name: Sort + two pointers
approaches.idea: Sort (value, index) pairs, then move pointers inward from both ends. Works, but sorting costs O(n log n) and you must carry the original indices.

approaches.name: One-pass hash map
approaches.idea: Scan once; for each x check whether target − x is already in the map, otherwise store x → index.

solution.summary: Scan the array once with a hash map from value to index; for each number check whether its complement target − x was already seen. That is O(n) time and O(n) space instead of the O(n²) pair check.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A pair (a, b) works when b = target − a. So at every position the question is not "which pair?" but "have I already seen the one number I need?" — a perfect job for a hash map with O(1) average lookups.

**Algorithm**
1. Create `seen`: value → index of every element to the **left** of i.
2. For each index i compute `need = target − nums[i]`.
3. If `need` is in `seen`, return `[seen[need], i]`.
4. Otherwise store `nums[i] → i` and continue.

**Why it is correct.** When the scan reaches the second element of the answer pair, the first one is already in the map, so it is found. Checking *before* inserting means an element is never paired with itself (target 6, value 3), while two different 3s still work because the first one was stored earlier.

**Edge cases:** duplicates ([3, 3]), negatives and zero (pure arithmetic, no special handling), and the pair at the very end.

**Talk track:** state the O(n²) brute force, point out the repeated work (searching for the partner again and again), then use the map to make that search O(1).

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average map operations
complexity.space: O(n) — the map can hold every element

keyPoints: Start from the O(n²) brute force, then remove the repeated search
Complement lookup: need = target − x
Check before inserting so an element never pairs with itself
Hash map trades O(n) space for O(n) time
Sorting loses the original indices and costs O(n log n)

visuals.title: One-pass hash map on nums = [6, 13, 2, 9, 5, 11], target = 14
visuals.caption: Blue = current index, light blue = already stored in the map, green = the answer pair.

steps.note: Start with an empty map `seen` (value → index). It will hold every number to the **left** of the current index.
i = 0: need = 14 − 6 = 8. 8 has not been seen, so remember 6 → 0.
i = 1: need = 14 − 13 = 1. 1 has not been seen, so remember 13 → 1.
i = 2: need = 14 − 2 = 12. 12 has not been seen, so remember 2 → 2.
i = 3: need = 14 − 9 = 5. 5 has not been seen, so remember 9 → 3.
i = 4: need = 14 − 5 = 9, and **9 is in `seen` at index 3**. Return [3, 4].

columns: When it is the right call
rows: Only as the first thing you say

pitfalls: Inserting before checking, which pairs an element with itself when target = 2·x
Returning the values instead of the indices

followUps.question: What if the array is sorted?
followUps.answer: Use two pointers from both ends: move left up if the sum is too small, right down if too big. O(n) time, O(1) space.

followUps.question: What if you must return every pair (values may repeat)?
followUps.answer: Count occurrences in a map; for each distinct x with x < target − x there are count[x] · count[target − x] pairs, and when x = target − x there are c·(c−1)/2 (c = count[x]). Or sort and use two pointers, skipping duplicates.

followUps.question: What about 3Sum?
followUps.answer: Sort, fix one element, and run two pointers on the rest: O(n²). Skip equal neighbours to avoid duplicate triples.

questions.title: Contains Duplicate
questions.prompt: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if **some value occurs at least twice**, and `false` if every value is distinct.

examples.explanation: 9 appears at indices 1 and 4.

hints: Comparing every pair works but is O(n²). n can be 10⁵.
After sorting, where must equal values be?
Remember what you have seen in a structure with O(1) membership checks.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Compare every pair i < j.

approaches.name: Sort and compare neighbours
approaches.idea: After sorting, duplicates are adjacent, so one pass over nums[i] === nums[i − 1] finds them.

approaches.name: Hash set
approaches.idea: Add values to a set while scanning; a value already in the set is a duplicate.

solution.summary: Walk through the array keeping a hash set of values seen so far; the first value that is already in the set is a duplicate. O(n) time and O(n) space, with an early exit.
solution.explanation:
**Algorithm**
1. Start with an empty set `seen`.
2. For each x: if x is in `seen` return true, otherwise add it.
3. If the loop finishes, all values were distinct: return false.

**Why a set?** Membership checks and inserts are O(1) on average, so the whole scan is O(n). It also stops at the first duplicate, which helps when duplicates are early.

**Trade-off with sorting.** Sorting then checking neighbours uses O(1) extra space (with an in-place sort such as heapsort) but O(n log n) time, and it modifies the input. Say both and let the interviewer choose: "If memory is tight, sort; otherwise the set is faster."

**One-liners** (fine to mention, but explain the cost): Python `len(set(nums)) != len(nums)`, JS `new Set(nums).size !== nums.length` — both O(n), but they always process the whole array.

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass with O(1) average set operations
complexity.space: O(n) — the set may store every value

keyPoints: Hash set gives O(1) average "seen before?" checks
Early exit at the first duplicate
Sorting alternative: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, mutates input
Java's Set.add returns false when the value is already present

visuals.title: Hash-set scan on nums = [4, 9, 2, 7, 9, 1]
visuals.caption: Blue = current element, light blue = already in the set, green = the duplicate pair, grey = never examined.

steps.note: Scan left to right with an empty set `seen`. A set answers "have I met this value?" in O(1) on average.
i = 0: 4 is not in the set, so add it. Each check and add is O(1) on average.
i = 1: 9 is not in the set, so add it.
i = 2: 2 is not in the set, so add it.
i = 3: 7 is not in the set, so add it.
i = 4: x = 9 is **already in the set** (it was at index 1). Return true immediately — no need to look at the rest.

visuals.title: Time vs memory trade-off
rows: ≈5 × 10⁹ pair checks for n = 10⁵: too slow
Mutates the input (copy it if that is not allowed)
Fastest; stops at the first duplicate

pitfalls: Using arr.includes / indexOf inside the loop — that is O(n²)
Sorting the caller's array without asking whether mutation is allowed
Forgetting the early return and always scanning the whole array

followUps.question: Duplicates within distance k (|i − j| ≤ k)?
followUps.answer: Keep a map value → last index (or a sliding-window set of size k); a duplicate counts if i − last[x] ≤ k. O(n) time.

followUps.question: What if the values are in the range 1..n?
followUps.answer: Use a boolean array of size n + 1 instead of a hash set (faster, no hashing), or mark visited by negating nums[|x| − 1] for O(1) extra space if mutation is allowed.

questions.title: Valid Anagram
questions.prompt:
Two strings are **anagrams** when one can be rearranged into the other: they use exactly the same letters, each the same number of times.

Given strings `s` and `t`, return `true` if `t` is an anagram of `s`, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: t contains 'c', which s does not.
Same letters, different counts.

constraints: s and t contain lowercase English letters
hints: Two anagrams have the same multiset of characters. How can you compare multisets?
Sorting both strings works. Can you avoid the O(n log n)?
Count characters of s up, count characters of t down; every count must end at 0.

approaches.name: Sort both
approaches.idea: Sort the characters of both strings and compare.

approaches.name: Count with a map
approaches.idea: Count characters of s, then decrement for t; a count that would go below 0 means not an anagram.

approaches.name: Count with a 26-slot array
approaches.idea: Same idea with int[26] indexed by ch − 'a' for lowercase letters: no hashing, constant space.

solution.summary: If the lengths differ, return false. Otherwise count each character of s, then walk t and decrement; if t ever needs a character whose count is already 0, it is not an anagram. O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet.
solution.explanation:
**Idea.** Anagrams have identical character frequencies. Build the frequencies of s, then "spend" them while reading t.

**Steps**
1. Different lengths → `false` immediately.
2. For each ch in s: `count[ch]++`.
3. For each ch in t: if `count[ch]` is 0 (or missing) → `false`; else `count[ch]--`.
4. Return `true`.

**Why step 3 is enough.** Lengths are equal, so if no count ever goes negative, the totals match exactly and every count ends at 0. There is no need for a final loop over the map.

**Fixed alphabet.** For lowercase English letters, replace the map with `int[26]` indexed by `ch − 'a'`: O(1) space, faster in practice. A map version (shown) also works for any Unicode text.

**Unicode follow-up:** in JavaScript `for...of` iterates code points, so emoji count as one character; Java's `char` is a UTF-16 unit, so use `codePoints()` when surrogate pairs matter.

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass over each string
complexity.space: O(1) — at most 26 keys for lowercase letters (O(k) for k distinct characters in general)

keyPoints: Length check first
Count up for s, down for t; fail as soon as a count would go negative
int[26] array for a fixed alphabet: O(1) space
Sorting is the O(n log n) alternative

visuals.caption: Blue = current character, light blue = already processed. The map shows how many unmatched copies of each character s still has.

steps.note: Lengths are equal (5), so keep going. Count every character of s in `count`.
s[0] = 's': count['s'] becomes 1.
s[1] = 't': count['t'] becomes 1.
s[2] = 'o': count['o'] becomes 1.
s[3] = 'n': count['n'] becomes 1.
s[4] = 'e': count['e'] becomes 1. s is fully counted.
t[0] = 'n': count['n'] was 1, so s still had a spare 'n'. Use it: 0.
t[1] = 'o': count['o'] was 1, so s still had a spare 'o'. Use it: 0.
t[2] = 't': count['t'] was 1, so s still had a spare 't'. Use it: 0.
t[3] = 'e': count['e'] was 1, so s still had a spare 'e'. Use it: 0.
t[4] = 's': count['s'] was 1, so s still had a spare 's'. Use it: 0.
Every character of t was matched by one from s, and the lengths are equal, so every count is back to 0. **Return true.**

visuals.title: isAnagram("rat", "car") → false (early exit)
visuals.caption: Red = the first character of t that s cannot supply.

steps.note: Lengths are equal (3), so keep going. Count every character of s in `count`.
s[0] = 'r': count['r'] becomes 1.
s[1] = 'a': count['a'] becomes 1.
s[2] = 't': count['t'] becomes 1. s is fully counted.
t[0] = 'c': count['c'] is missing (0), so t has a 'c' that s cannot match. **Return false** without reading the rest of t.

pitfalls: Forgetting the length check, so "ab" vs "a" looks fine
Comparing only the set of letters, not the counts ("aab" vs "abb")
Using a 26-slot array when the input can contain uppercase letters or Unicode

followUps.question: Find all anagrams of p inside a longer string s?
followUps.answer: Sliding window of length |p| with a 26-count array; compare counts (or track a "matches" counter) as the window moves: O(n).

followUps.question: Minimum deletions to make two strings anagrams?
followUps.answer: Count both strings; the answer is the sum over letters of |countS − countT|.

questions.title: Group Anagrams
questions.prompt: Given a list of lowercase words `strs`, put words that are **anagrams of each other** (same letters, same counts) into the same group. Return the list of groups; the order of groups and of words inside a group does not matter.
hints: Checking every pair of words with an anagram test is O(n²·k). Can each word compute something on its own?
All words in one group should map to the same "canonical" value.
Sort each word's letters (or count them) and use that as a hash map key.

approaches.name: Pairwise comparison
approaches.idea: Compare every word with every group representative using an anagram check.

approaches.name: Sorted-letters key
approaches.idea: key = sorted letters of the word; group words in a map by key.

approaches.name: Letter-count key
approaches.idea: key = the 26 letter counts (e.g. joined with "#"); building it is O(k).

solution.summary: Give every word a canonical key that is identical for all its anagrams — its letters sorted — and group words in a hash map from key to list. That is O(n·k log k), or O(n·k) with a 26-letter count as the key.
solution.explanation:
**Key idea: canonical form.** Instead of comparing words with each other, transform each word into a representation shared by exactly its anagrams. Two common choices:
- **Sorted letters**: "study" → "dstuy". Simple and readable.
- **Letter counts**: 26 numbers, e.g. `count.join('#')`. Building it is O(k) instead of O(k log k).

**Algorithm**
1. `groups` = empty map from key → list of words.
2. For each word, compute its key and append the word to `groups[key]`.
3. Return all the lists.

**Complexity.** n words of length up to k: sorting each word costs O(k log k), so O(n·k log k) total; the count key gives O(n·k). With k ≤ 100 the difference is small — mention it, but either is accepted.

**Count key in JavaScript** (O(k) per word):
```js
const count = new Array(26).fill(0);
for (const ch of word) count[ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97]++;
const key = count.join('#'); // separator avoids "1,11" vs "11,1" clashes
```

**Do not** use the sum or product of character codes as the key: different words can share a sum ("ad" and "bc"), and products overflow.

complexity.time: O(n · k log k) — sort each of n words of length k (O(n · k) with a count key)
complexity.space: O(n · k) — the map stores every word and key

keyPoints: Map each word to a canonical key shared by all its anagrams
Sorted letters: O(k log k) per word; 26-count signature: O(k)
Hash map from key to list of words
Use a separator in the count key; never use sums of character codes

visuals.title: Grouping by sorted-letter key
visuals.caption: Blue = current word, yellow = earlier words with the same key, light blue = other processed words.

steps.note: Anagrams contain the same letters, so **sorting the letters** gives every member of a group the same key. Use the key to bucket words in a map.
"dusty" → key "dstuy". No group has this key yet, so start a new one.
"night" → key "ghint". No group has this key yet, so start a new one.
"study" → key "dstuy" — the **same key** as "dusty", so it joins that group in O(1).
"arc" → key "acr". No group has this key yet, so start a new one.
"thing" → key "ghint" — the **same key** as "night", so it joins that group in O(1).
"car" → key "acr" — the **same key** as "arc", so it joins that group in O(1).
Return the map's values: [dusty, study], [night, thing], [arc, car]. 6 words, 3 groups, one pass.

visuals.title: Choosing the key
rows: Yes — optimal for a fixed alphabet

pitfalls: Using a key that is not unique per anagram class (sum of codes)
Building a count key without separators, so counts like 1,11 and 11,1 collide
Comparing words pairwise (O(n²))
Forgetting the empty string, which is its own group

followUps.question: What if words can contain any Unicode characters?
followUps.answer: Sorted-letters still works (sort code points); a fixed 26-slot count does not — use a map of character counts serialized in sorted key order.

followUps.question: How would you do this for a stream of millions of words?
followUps.answer: Same key, but store groups in a key-value store (or shard by key hash) so each word is processed independently: a natural map-reduce, with the key as the reducer key.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **k values that occur most often**. Any order is accepted, and the input guarantees the answer is unique (no tie at the k-th place).

Can you beat O(n log n)?

examples.explanation: 5 appears 4 times, 3 appears 3 times, 1 and 7 once.

hints: Start by counting how often each value appears.
Sorting the (value, count) pairs works in O(n log n). Do you need a full sort to get only the top k?
A count is always between 1 and n. Use the count itself as an array index (bucket sort), or keep a min-heap of size k.

approaches.name: Count + sort
approaches.idea: Count with a map, sort distinct values by count descending, take the first k.

approaches.name: Count + min-heap of size k
approaches.idea: Push each distinct value into a min-heap ordered by count; pop whenever the size exceeds k. The heap ends with the top k.

approaches.name: Count + bucket sort
approaches.idea: buckets[c] = values with count c (c ≤ n). Walk buckets from n down to 1 and collect k values.

solution.summary: Count frequencies with a hash map, then bucket the values by their count — counts are between 1 and n, so an array of n + 1 buckets replaces sorting — and read buckets from the highest count down until I have k values. O(n) time and space; a size-k min-heap is the O(n log k) alternative.
solution.explanation:
**Step 1 — count.** `freq[x]` = number of occurrences. O(n).

**Step 2 — bucket by count.** Create `buckets[0..n]`. For each (x, c) put x into `buckets[c]`. Because every count is an integer in 1..n, the bucket index *is* the sort key — no comparison sort needed. O(n).

**Step 3 — collect.** Walk c from n down to 1, appending values until there are k. O(n) total, since there are n + 1 buckets and at most n values.

**Heap alternative (often what interviewers expect first).** Keep a **min-heap of size k** keyed by count: push each distinct value, and if the heap grows past k pop the smallest. The heap always holds the best k seen so far → O(n log k). Useful when k is tiny compared to n, or when data arrives as a stream (bucket sort needs to know n up front).
- Java: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> freq.get(a) - freq.get(b))`, offer, and poll when `size() > k`.
- Python: `heapq.nlargest(k, freq.keys(), key=freq.get)`.

**Quickselect** on the distinct values by count gives O(n) average too, but is harder to code correctly in an interview.

complexity.time: O(n) — counting, bucketing and collecting are each linear
complexity.space: O(n) — the frequency map and n + 1 buckets

keyPoints: Always count first with a hash map
Counts are bounded by n → bucket sort in O(n)
Min-heap of size k → O(n log k); evict the least frequent
Full sort O(n log n) is the baseline to beat
Heap works for streams; buckets need n up front

visuals.title: Bucket sort by frequency, k = 2
visuals.caption: Bottom row: buckets[c] lists the values that occur exactly c times (· = empty). Reading it right to left gives values from most to least frequent.

steps.note: Find the k = 2 most frequent values. First count each value — a frequency can be at most n = 9, which is what makes bucket sort possible.
One pass fills `freq`: 5 appears 4×, 3 appears 3×, 1 appears 1×, 7 appears 1×.
5 has count 4, so it goes into bucket 4. The index **is** the frequency, so no sorting is needed.
3 has count 3, so it goes into bucket 3. The index **is** the frequency, so no sorting is needed.
1 has count 1, so it goes into bucket 1. The index **is** the frequency, so no sorting is needed.
7 has count 1, so it goes into bucket 1. Bucket 1 now holds 1 and 7 — ties share a bucket. The index **is** the frequency, so no sorting is needed.
Walk the buckets from the highest count down. Buckets 5–9 are empty, so they are skipped.
c = 4: take 5 (the most frequent value). The result has 1 of 2.
c = 3: take 3. The result has k = 2 values, so **return [5, 3]** without touching the remaining buckets.

visuals.title: Sort vs heap vs buckets
rows: Simplest to write; fine for moderate n
k ≪ n, or values arrive as a stream
Mention only; tricky to get right under pressure

pitfalls: Pushing every distinct value into a max-heap one at a time (O(n log n)) when a min-heap of size k gives O(n log k)
Sizing buckets by the number of distinct values instead of n + 1 (a count can be n)
Returning counts instead of values
Comparator overflow in Java (a − b) with huge counts — fine here because counts ≤ 10⁵

followUps.question: Top k frequent words, ties broken alphabetically?
followUps.answer: Use a heap with comparator (count, then reverse alphabetical for the min-heap), or sort the (count desc, word asc) pairs: O(n log k) / O(n log n).

followUps.question: What if the data is an endless stream?
followUps.answer: Exact answers need all counts (a map) plus a heap; for bounded memory use approximate sketches such as Count-Min Sketch with a heap of heavy hitters.

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the **product of every element except nums[i]**.

Do it in O(n) time **without using division**. Follow-up: use only O(1) extra space (the output array does not count).

examples.explanation: Only the zero position avoids multiplying by 0.

constraints: Every prefix and suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Division would be easy — why is it banned? Think about zeros.
answer[i] = (product of the elements to its left) × (product of the elements to its right).
Fill answer with left products in one pass, then sweep from the right with a running suffix product.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For each i multiply all other elements.

approaches.name: Total product ÷ nums[i]
approaches.idea: Not allowed, and breaks with zeros (needs special cases for one zero vs two zeros).

approaches.name: Prefix and suffix arrays
approaches.idea: left[i] and right[i] arrays, answer[i] = left[i] × right[i].

approaches.name: Output as prefix array + running suffix
approaches.idea: Store left products directly in answer, then multiply by a running suffix variable from the right.

solution.summary: Every answer is the product of what is to its left times the product of what is to its right. I write the left products into the output in one pass, then sweep from the right keeping a running suffix product and multiply it in — O(n) time, O(1) extra space, no division.
solution.explanation:
**Decompose.** For index i: `answer[i] = (nums[0] × … × nums[i−1]) × (nums[i+1] × … × nums[n−1])`. Both parts are running products we can build incrementally.

**Pass 1 (left to right).** Keep `prefix` = product of everything before i. Write `answer[i] = prefix`, then `prefix *= nums[i]`.

**Pass 2 (right to left).** Keep `suffix` = product of everything after i. Do `answer[i] *= suffix`, then `suffix *= nums[i]`.

**Why not division?** With one zero the total product is 0. The non-zero positions correctly get 0, but the zero's own position would need 0 ÷ 0, while its real answer is the product of all the other elements. With two or more zeros every answer is 0. Handling that needs special cases, and the problem forbids division anyway.

**Space.** Two extra arrays (left, right) give O(n) space and are the easiest to explain first. Reusing `answer` for the left products and a single `suffix` variable gives **O(1) extra space**.

**Overflow.** The constraints guarantee the products fit in 32 bits; in general, use `long` (Java) or BigInt (JS) and mention it.

**JavaScript detail:** `0 * -3` is `-0`, so Node prints `-0` for some zeros in example 3. It is `=== 0` and `JSON.stringify` writes `0`, so the answer is still correct.

code.code:
def product_except_self(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    answer = [1] * n
    prefix = 1  # product of everything left of i
    for i in range(n):
        answer[i] = prefix
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1  # product of everything right of i
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        answer[i] *= suffix
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return answer

No division: zeros break it

Left pass, i = 0: answer[0] = prefix = 1 (nothing is left of index 0). Then prefix *= 2 → 2.
Left pass, i = 1: answer[1] = prefix = 2 (= 2). Then prefix *= 3 → 6.
Left pass, i = 2: answer[2] = prefix = 6 (= 2 × 3). Then prefix *= 4 → 24.
Left pass, i = 3: answer[3] = prefix = 24 (= 2 × 3 × 4). Then prefix *= 5 → 120.
Right pass, i = 3: answer[3] = 24 × suffix 1 (nothing is right of the last index) = **24**. Then suffix *= 5 → 5.
Right pass, i = 2: answer[2] = 6 × suffix 5 (= 5) = **30**. Then suffix *= 4 → 20.
Right pass, i = 1: answer[1] = 2 × suffix 20 (= 4 × 5) = **40**. Then suffix *= 3 → 60.
Right pass, i = 0: answer[0] = 1 × suffix 60 (= 3 × 4 × 5) = **60**. Then suffix *= 2 → 120.
Done: [60, 40, 30, 24]. Each answer combines its left product (first pass) and right product (second pass). O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output.

Right products: right[i] = nums[i+1] × … × nums[n−1], with right[last] = 1. Every cell before the 0 becomes 0.

Starting the right pass with the wrong suffix (it must be 1, not nums[n−1])

questions.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
questions.prompt:
Given an **unsorted** integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest run of **consecutive integers** (x, x+1, x+2, …) whose values all appear in the array. The values can be in any positions; duplicates count once.

Your algorithm must run in **O(n)** time.

examples.explanation: The run 1, 2, 3, 4.
The run -1, 0, 1, 2 (the duplicate 2 counts once).

hints: Sorting solves it in O(n log n). What do you need to know about a number to extend a run without sorting?
With a set, "is x + 1 present?" is O(1).
Only start counting from numbers x where x − 1 is not in the set; otherwise you recount the same run.

approaches.name: Sort and scan
approaches.idea: Sort, then walk counting runs of +1 steps and skipping duplicates.

approaches.name: Set, extend from every number
approaches.idea: For each x count x+1, x+2, … in the set. Correct but recounts runs: O(n²) on one long run.

approaches.name: Set, extend only from run starts
approaches.idea: Skip x when x − 1 is present; every run is walked once from its smallest element.

solution.summary: Put all numbers in a hash set, and only start counting at numbers x whose predecessor x − 1 is missing — the start of a run. From each start, walk x+1, x+2, … in the set. Every element is visited a constant number of times, so it is O(n) time and O(n) space.
solution.explanation:
**Algorithm**
1. `set` = all values (also removes duplicates).
2. For each x in the set: if `x − 1` is in the set, skip — x is not a run start.
3. Otherwise count `length` while `x + length` is in the set.
4. Track the maximum.

**Why O(n) despite the nested while?** The while loop only runs from run starts, and runs are disjoint. Each value is "extended over" by at most one while loop, so the while bodies run at most n times **in total**, plus n iterations of the for loop → O(n). This is amortized reasoning — say it explicitly, because interviewers often ask.

**Iterate the set, not the array.** If you loop over `nums` and a run start appears many times (e.g. 50,000 copies of 1 followed by 2..50,001), you would walk the same run once per copy — O(n²).

**Sorting alternative:** O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space if in-place sorting is allowed. Mention it as the trade-off.

complexity.time: O(n) — each value is visited by the for loop once and by at most one while loop

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.prompt: Given an integer array `nums` (values may be **negative**) and an integer `k`, return **how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays** have a sum exactly equal to `k`.

examples.explanation: [0] twice and [0, 0].

hints: The brute force fixes a start and extends the end with a running sum: O(n²). Can you avoid fixing the start?
Let prefix[i] be the sum of nums[0..i]. What is the sum of nums[j+1..i] in terms of prefixes?
Count how many earlier prefixes equal prefix − k with a hash map, and seed it with {0: 1}.

approaches.name: All subarrays, sum each
approaches.idea: Three nested loops.

approaches.name: Fix the start, running sum
approaches.idea: For each start, extend the end while adding to a running sum.

approaches.name: Sliding window
approaches.idea: Does not work: with negative numbers, adding an element can decrease the sum, so you cannot tell when to shrink.

approaches.name: Prefix sum + hash map
approaches.idea: sum(j+1..i) = prefix[i] − prefix[j]. For each i add the number of earlier prefixes equal to prefix[i] − k.

solution.summary: A subarray ending at i sums to k when prefix[i] − prefix[j] = k for some earlier j. So while scanning I keep a hash map of how many times each prefix sum has occurred, add map[prefix − k] to the answer at every index, and seed the map with {0: 1} for subarrays that start at index 0. O(n) time and space.
solution.explanation:
**Prefix sums.** Let `prefix[i] = nums[0] + … + nums[i]`. The sum of `nums[j+1..i]` is `prefix[i] − prefix[j]`.

**Turn it into a lookup.** We want `prefix[i] − prefix[j] = k` ⇔ `prefix[j] = prefix[i] − k`. So at each i, the number of good subarrays ending at i equals **how many earlier prefixes equal prefix[i] − k** — a Two Sum style complement lookup, but counting.

**Algorithm**
1. `seen = {0: 1}` — the empty prefix, so a subarray starting at index 0 (prefix[i] = k) is counted.
2. For each x: `prefix += x`; `count += seen[prefix − k]`; then `seen[prefix]++`.
3. Return `count`.

**Order matters:** look up before inserting the current prefix, otherwise k = 0 would count the empty subarray.

**Why not a sliding window?** A window needs "growing increases the sum, shrinking decreases it". Negative numbers break that monotonicity. (If all numbers are positive, a sliding window gives O(1) space.)

**Edge cases:** zeros and k = 0 (several prefixes can repeat — that is why we store counts, not indices), negative k, a single element.

code.code:
def subarray_sum(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    seen = {0: 1}  # prefix sum -> how many times seen
    prefix = 0
    count = 0
    for x in nums:
        prefix += x
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)  # subarrays ending here with sum k
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count

complexity.time: O(n) — one pass, O(1) average map operations
complexity.space: O(n) — up to n distinct prefix sums

Count earlier prefixes equal to prefix − k with a hash map

Sliding window fails with negative numbers

i = 0: prefix = 2, need = 2 − 3 = -1. Not seen, so no subarray ending here sums to 3. Record prefix 2.
i = 1: prefix = 1, need = 1 − 3 = -2. Not seen, so no subarray ending here sums to 3. Record prefix 1.
i = 2: prefix = 4, need = 4 − 3 = 1, seen 1× → **1 subarray** ending here: [3]. count = 1. Then record prefix 4 in `seen`.
i = 3: prefix = 5, need = 5 − 3 = 2, seen 1× → **1 subarray** ending here: [-1, 3, 1]. count = 2. Then record prefix 5 in `seen`.

i = 4: prefix = 3, need = 3 − 3 = 0, seen 1× → **1 subarray** ending here: [2, -1, 3, 1, -2]. count = 3. This one starts at index 0 — that is why {0: 1} is in the map from the start. Then record prefix 3 in `seen`.
i = 5: prefix = 7, need = 7 − 3 = 4, seen 1× → **1 subarray** ending here: [1, -2, 4]. count = 4. Then record prefix 7 in `seen`.
Total **4** subarrays sum to 3: [3], [-1, 3, 1], [2, -1, 3, 1, -2], [1, -2, 4]. One pass, O(n) — and it works with negative numbers, unlike a sliding window.

followUps.answer: Store the first index of each prefix (never overwrite); length = i − first[prefix − k]. Seed with {0: −1}.

followUps.answer: Same idea with prefix mod k (normalize negative remainders): count earlier prefixes with the same remainder.

questions.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's algorithm)
questions.prompt: Given an integer array `nums` with at least one element, find the contiguous, non-empty subarray with the **largest sum** and return that sum.

examples.explanation: All negative: the best is the single largest element.
The whole array.

hints: Brute force: every start and end with a running sum, O(n²).
Think about the best subarray that ends exactly at index i. How does it relate to the best one ending at i − 1?
It either extends the previous one or starts fresh at nums[i] — whichever is larger.

approaches.name: All subarrays
approaches.idea: Fix a start, extend the end with a running sum, track the maximum.

approaches.name: Divide and conquer
approaches.idea: Best of left half, right half, and the best sum crossing the middle.

approaches.name: Kadane's algorithm
approaches.idea: current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i]); best = max(best, current).

solution.summary: Kadane's algorithm: keep the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index — either extend the previous one or restart at the current element, whichever is larger — and track the overall maximum. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**DP view.** Let `dp[i]` be the maximum sum of a subarray that **ends at i**. That subarray either is just `nums[i]`, or extends the best one ending at i − 1:

`dp[i] = max(nums[i], dp[i−1] + nums[i])`, and the answer is `max(dp)`.

Only `dp[i−1]` is needed, so keep one variable `current` → O(1) space.

**Intuition.** If the running sum so far is negative, it can only hurt whatever comes next — drop it and restart. If it is positive, keep extending, even through some negative numbers (like −1 in the example), because a later gain may outweigh them.

**Initialisation matters.** Start with `current = best = nums[0]`, not 0. Starting at 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array, but the subarray must be non-empty, so the answer is the largest single element (−1 for [−3, −1, −2]).

**Returning the indices:** remember `start` whenever you restart, and copy `(start, i)` into the best range when `best` improves.

code.code:
def max_sub_array(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    current = nums[0]  # best sum of a subarray that ends at i
    best = nums[0]
    for i in range(1, len(nums)):  # index loop: nums[1:] would copy the list
        current = max(nums[i], current + nums[i])  # restart or extend
        best = max(best, current)
    return best

questions.title: How does a hash map work internally?
questions.prompt: Explain how a hash map (Java `HashMap`, JavaScript `Map`, Python `dict`) stores and finds a key. Cover **hashing, buckets, collisions** (chaining vs open addressing), the **load factor and resizing**, and why operations are O(1) on average but O(n) in the worst case.
hints: Arrays give O(1) access by index. How do you turn an arbitrary key into an index?
Two different keys can produce the same index. What must the bucket store so you can tell them apart?
What happens to chain lengths as you keep inserting into a fixed number of buckets?

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "It stores key-value pairs and lookups are O(1)." No hashing, no collisions, no resizing, and no idea when it degrades.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Walks through hash → index → bucket, explains collisions with chaining and open addressing, load factor and doubling with rehash, the equals/hashCode contract, and average O(1) vs worst O(n) (Java 8 treeification).

solution.summary: A hash map is an array of buckets. It hashes the key to an integer, maps that to an index (hash mod capacity), and stores the entry in that bucket; different keys that land in the same bucket are kept in a chain (or in the next free slot with open addressing) and told apart with equals. Keeping the load factor low by doubling and rehashing keeps buckets short, so get/put are O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case.
solution.explanation:
**1. Hashing.** A hash function turns a key into an integer, deterministically (same key → same hash). Java calls `key.hashCode()`; strings use a polynomial like `s[0]·31ⁿ⁻¹ + … + s[n−1]`. A good hash spreads keys evenly.

**2. Index.** `index = hash mod capacity`. Java's HashMap keeps the capacity a power of two (default 16) and computes `(h ^ (h >>> 16)) & (capacity − 1)`, which is the same as a mod but faster and mixes the high bits in.

**3. Collisions.** Different keys can land in the same bucket (there are far more keys than buckets — pigeonhole principle).
- **Separate chaining**: each bucket holds a list of entries; lookup walks the list comparing keys with `equals`. Java's HashMap does this, and since Java 8 turns a long chain (8+ entries, table ≥ 64) into a red-black tree.
- **Open addressing**: entries live in the array itself; on a collision, probe other slots (linear probing: i+1, i+2, …). Deletions need **tombstones**. Python's dict uses open addressing.

**4. Load factor and resizing.** load factor = size ÷ buckets. When it passes a threshold (Java: **0.75**), allocate a bigger array (Java doubles) and **rehash** every entry because the index depends on the capacity. That single resize is O(n), but it happens rarely, so inserts stay **O(1) amortized**.

**5. Complexity.** Average O(1) for get/put/remove when the hash spreads keys well. Worst case **O(n)** when many keys collide (bad hash or adversarial input — "HashDoS"). Java 8+ limits this to O(log n) per bucket via treeification for Comparable keys.

**6. Keys in Java.** Override **both** `equals` and `hashCode` (equal objects must have equal hash codes), and do not mutate a key after inserting it — its hash changes and the entry becomes unreachable. Records do this correctly:
```java
// Custom keys must override BOTH equals() and hashCode().
// A record generates both from its fields.
record Point(int x, int y) {}

Map<Point, String> board = new HashMap<>();
board.put(new Point(1, 2), "treasure");
board.get(new Point(1, 2)); // "treasure": equal objects -> equal hash codes
```

**Ordering:** a plain hash map has no useful order. JavaScript `Map` and Python `dict` iterate in insertion order; Java has `LinkedHashMap` for that and `TreeMap` for sorted keys (O(log n)).

steps.note: An empty map: an array of 4 **buckets**, each a list (chain) of [key, value] entries. The load factor (size ÷ buckets) may not exceed 0.75.
set("apple", 5): hash = 93029210, index = 93029210 % 4 = **2**. Bucket 2 is empty: store the entry.
set("pear", 12): hash = 3436774, index = 3436774 % 4 = **2**. Bucket 2 already holds "apple" — a **collision**. The keys differ, so append to the chain.
set("kiwi", 7): hash = 3292336, index = 3292336 % 4 = **0**. Bucket 0 is empty: store the entry.
set("lime", 3): hash = 3321813, index = 3321813 % 4 = **1**. Bucket 1 is empty: store the entry. Size is now 4 and 4 / 4 = 1.0 > 0.75.

Load factor 4/4 = 1 > 0.75, so **resize**: allocate 8 buckets and re-insert every entry, because index = hash % capacity changes (apple: 2 → 2, pear: 2 → 6, kiwi: 0 → 0, lime: 1 → 5). The apple/pear collision disappears.
set("mango", 9): hash = 103662530, index = 103662530 % 8 = **2**. Bucket 2 already holds "apple" — a **collision**. The keys differ, so append to the chain.
get("mango"): hash → index 2. Walk the chain "apple" → "mango" comparing keys with ===; "mango" is entry #2. Return 9. With short chains this is O(1) on average.
set("apple", 6): the key is already in bucket 2, so the value is **overwritten** — size stays 5. A map never stores the same key twice.
Final state: 5 entries in 8 buckets (load 0.63). Average chain length stays below 1, so get/set are **O(1) on average**; a resize costs O(n) but happens rarely (amortized O(1)).

steps.note: Open addressing stores entries **in the array itself** (8 slots here). On a collision, probe the next slot (linear probing) until a free one is found.
insert "apple": hash % 8 = 2, slot 2 is free → store it there.
insert "mango": home slot 2 is taken. Probe forward → slot 3 (1 extra probe). Keys bunch together into a **cluster**.
insert "grape": home slot 3 is taken. Probe forward → slot 4 (1 extra probe). Keys bunch together into a **cluster**.
insert "kiwi": hash % 8 = 0, slot 0 is free → store it there.
delete "mango" from slot 3. We cannot just empty the slot: "grape" sits further along the same probe path. Leave a **tombstone** (DEL) instead.
get("grape"): home slot 3 holds a tombstone, so keep probing → found at slot 4. Had slot 3 been emptied, the search would have stopped there and wrongly reported "missing".
Open addressing is cache-friendly (one array, no pointers) but clusters grow quickly as the table fills, so these tables resize at a lower load factor (Python's dict at about 2/3).

followUps.question: Why is the capacity a power of two in Java?
followUps.answer: So hash mod capacity can be computed as hash & (capacity − 1), which is faster than %. Java first XORs the high 16 bits into the low bits so keys that differ only in high bits still spread out.

followUps.question: Is Java HashMap thread-safe?
followUps.answer: No. Concurrent writes can lose updates or corrupt the table. Use ConcurrentHashMap (fine-grained locking/CAS), not Collections.synchronizedMap for high concurrency.

followUps.question: HashMap vs TreeMap vs LinkedHashMap?
followUps.answer: HashMap: O(1) average, no order. LinkedHashMap: same plus insertion (or access) order — basis of a simple LRU cache. TreeMap: red-black tree, O(log n), sorted keys and range queries.

questions.title: Valid Sudoku
questions.prompt:
You are given a 9 × 9 Sudoku board as a grid of characters. Every cell is either a digit `'1'`–`'9'` or `'.'` for an empty cell.

Return `true` if the **filled cells** break none of these rules, otherwise `false`:
- no digit appears twice in the same **row**;
- no digit appears twice in the same **column**;
- no digit appears twice in the same **3 × 3 box** (the nine non-overlapping boxes).

Only check the digits that are already on the board. The board does **not** have to be solvable, and empty cells are ignored.

The examples draw the board with `|` and `-` between the boxes only to make it readable; rows and columns are numbered from 0.

examples.explanation: Every row, every column and every 3 × 3 box contains each digit at most once.

examples.input: the board from Example 1 with board[5][7] = '8'
examples.explanation: Row 5 and column 7 have no other 8, but the box covering rows 3–5 and columns 6–8 already has an 8 at (3, 6). A solution that checks only rows and columns would wrongly return `true`.

examples.input: the board from Example 1 with board[8][2] = '3'
examples.explanation: Column 2 now holds a 3 in row 0 and another in row 8.

hints: There are 27 groups to check: 9 rows, 9 columns and 9 boxes. Which data structure answers "have I already seen this digit in this group?" in O(1)?
Keep one set per row, one per column and one per box, and fill all of them during a single scan of the board.
To find the box of cell (r, c), number the boxes 0–8 row by row: b = Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3).

approaches.name: Brute force: scan the groups of every cell
approaches.idea: For each filled cell, walk its row, its column and its box looking for the same digit.
approaches.time: O(n³) — each of the n² cells scans 3 groups of n cells

approaches.name: Three separate passes
approaches.idea: Check the 9 rows, then the 9 columns, then the 9 boxes, each with a fresh set. Correct, but it is three nearly identical loops, and the box loop needs extra index arithmetic.
approaches.space: O(n) — one set at a time

approaches.name: One pass, 27 sets
approaches.idea: Scan once; each digit is checked against and added to rows[r], cols[c] and boxes[b], with b = Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3).

solution.summary: Scan the board once and keep 27 hash sets: one per row, one per column and one per 3 × 3 box. For a digit at (r, c) the box is b = Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3); if the digit is already in rows[r], cols[c] or boxes[b] the board is invalid, otherwise I add it to all three. For a fixed 9 × 9 board that is constant time and space.
solution.explanation:
**Idea.** A board is valid when each of its 27 groups (9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes) has no repeated digit. That is the *Contains Duplicate* problem 27 times, so use one hash set per group and fill them all in a single pass.

**Box index.** Number the boxes 0–8 left to right, top to bottom. Row `r` is in band `Math.floor(r / 3)` (0, 1 or 2) and column `c` is in band `Math.floor(c / 3)`. Each band of rows holds 3 boxes, so

`b = Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3)`

Example: (5, 7) → bands 1 and 2 → b = 1 · 3 + 2 = **5**. It is the same formula you use to flatten a 2D index (`row * width + col`).

**Algorithm**
1. Create `rows`, `cols` and `boxes`: 9 empty sets each.
2. Visit every cell (r, c) and skip `'.'`.
3. Compute `b`. If the digit `d` is already in `rows[r]`, `cols[c]` or `boxes[b]`, return `false` immediately.
4. Otherwise add `d` to all three sets.
5. If the scan finishes, return `true`.

**Why it is correct.** If two equal digits share a group, whichever is scanned second finds the first one in that shared set. Digits in different groups never share a set, so they never cause a false alarm.

**Complexity.** The board is always 9 × 9, so strictly it is O(1) time and space. Say it like this in the interview: *"O(n²) for an n × n board — 81 cells here, so constant."*

**Edge cases.** An empty board (all `'.'`) is valid. A board can be valid and still unsolvable; this problem only checks the rules, it does not solve the puzzle.

complexity.time: O(n²) for an n × n board — each of the 81 cells is read once, so O(1) for a fixed 9 × 9 board
complexity.space: O(n²) — 27 sets holding at most 3 × 81 entries, again constant for 9 × 9

keyPoints: 27 groups — 9 rows, 9 columns, 9 boxes — and none may repeat a digit
One pass with a hash set per group; return false on the first repeat
Box index: Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3)
Skip '.' cells; valid does not mean solvable
O(81) = O(1) for a fixed board; O(n²) for an n × n board

visuals.title: One pass with 27 sets on Example 2 (rows 0–5 shown)
visuals.caption: Only rows 0–5 are drawn: the scan returns false in row 5, so rows 6–8 are never read. Blank = '.', blue = current cell, light blue = earlier digits already in rows[r], cols[c] or boxes[b], red = the clash.

steps.note: Create 27 empty sets: `rows[0..8]`, `cols[0..8]` and `boxes[0..8]`. The scan visits the cells row by row, left to right; a blank cell is `'.'`.
r = 0, c = 0: `d` is `'.'`, an empty cell, so `continue`. Empty cells can never clash, so they never go into a set.
(0, 2) holds `'3'` and lies in box b = 0 · 3 + 0 = 0. `rows[0]`, `cols[2]` and `boxes[0]` are all empty, so 3 is new: add it to all three sets.
(0, 3) = `'7'`. Column 3 starts the second box column, so b = 0 · 3 + Math.floor(3 / 3) = **1**. 7 is not in `rows[0]` = {3}, `cols[3]` or `boxes[1]`, so add it.

(1, 6) = `'1'`, box b = 0 · 3 + 2 = 2. There is already a 1 at (0, 5), but in a **different row, column and box**, so none of the three sets has it: `rows[1]` = {8, 2, 5, 4}, `cols[6]` = {}, `boxes[2]` = {}. Add 1.

Rows 1–2 are filled in the same way. (3, 6) = `'8'`, box b = Math.floor(3 / 3) · 3 + Math.floor(6 / 3) = 1 · 3 + 2 = **5**. 8 is new in `rows[3]` = {4, 9, 6, 3, 7}, `cols[6]` = {1} and `boxes[5]`, so add it. Remember this 8.

(4, 5) = `'8'` sits right next to the 8 at (3, 6), but it is in box b = 1 · 3 + 1 = **4**, another row and another column. `rows[4]` = {1}, `cols[5]` = {1, 7} and `boxes[4]` = {6, 3, 7, 1} have no 8, so it is legal. Add it.

(5, 7) = `'8'`, box b = 1 · 3 + 2 = 5. `rows[5]` = {2, 1, 4} and `cols[7]` = {4, 1, 9} have no 8, but **`boxes[5]` = {8, 1, 9} already holds the 8 from (3, 6)** → return `false`. A check of only rows and columns would miss this clash.

visuals.title: Box index b = Math.floor(r / 3) * 3 + Math.floor(c / 3)
visuals.caption: Each cell of this 3 × 3 table is one 3 × 3 box of the Sudoku. Rows of the table = Math.floor(r / 3), columns = Math.floor(c / 3), value = box number b.

steps.note: Number the 9 boxes 0–8 left to right, top to bottom. `Math.floor(r / 3)` says which band of rows a cell is in, `Math.floor(c / 3)` which band of columns. Each band of rows holds 3 boxes, hence the `* 3`.
(0, 3): Math.floor(0 / 3) = 0 and Math.floor(3 / 3) = 1, so b = 0 · 3 + 1 = **1** — the top-middle box.
(3, 6) and (5, 7) are in different rows and columns, but both give 1 · 3 + 2 = **5**. They share `boxes[5]`, which is exactly why their two 8s clash in Example 2.
(8, 0): 2 · 3 + 0 = **6**, the bottom-left box. Same idea as flattening a 2D index: row · width + column.

Common bug: `Math.floor(r / 3) + Math.floor(c / 3)` without the `* 3`. It produces only 5 different numbers, e.g. the top-middle and middle-left boxes both become 1, so digits from different boxes would share a set and cause false clashes.
With `* 3` every box gets its own number 0–8, so each digit lands in exactly one row set, one column set and one box set.

pitfalls: Using Math.floor(r / 3) + Math.floor(c / 3) as the box index: the top-middle and middle-left boxes both get number 1
Forgetting integer division: in JavaScript and Python 3, 5 / 3 is 1.666…, so use Math.floor or //
Checking only rows and columns, so a repeat inside a box (Example 2) slips through
Treating '.' like a digit, so two empty cells look like a duplicate

followUps.question: Can you use less memory?
followUps.answer: Replace each set with a 9-bit integer mask: bit d − 1 set means digit d was seen. Test with (mask >> (d − 1)) & 1, set with mask |= 1 << (d − 1). That is 27 integers instead of 27 sets.

followUps.question: How would you actually solve the Sudoku?
followUps.answer: Backtracking: pick an empty cell, try each digit that is not in its row, column and box sets, recurse, and undo the choice if the recursion fails. The same three sets make each check O(1).

followUps.question: Can you do it with a single set?
followUps.answer: Yes: store strings such as "8 in row 3", "8 in col 6" and "8 in box 5". Same O(81) work; a neat trick, but the three arrays of sets are easier to explain.

questions.title: Encode and Decode Strings
questions.prompt:
Design two functions:

- `encode(strs)` turns a **list of strings** into **one string**;
- `decode(encoded)` turns that string back into the **exact same list**.

The strings may contain **any character** — letters, digits, spaces, `'#'`, commas — and may be empty. `decode(encode(strs))` must equal `strs` for every possible list. Do not use a built-in serializer such as `JSON.stringify`, `pickle` or Java serialization: design the format yourself.

Think of it as sending a list of messages over a connection that can only carry a single string.

examples.explanation: The `'#'` inside "a#" and the digits in "12" are never misread: the decoder reads a length, then copies exactly that many characters without looking at them.
An empty list encodes to the empty string, while `[""]` encodes to `"0#"`, so the two stay different.

constraints: strs[i] may contain any character, including '#', digits and spaces
hints: Why does joining with a separator like ',' fail? Find two different lists that produce the same joined string.
The decoder must know where each string ends without looking inside it.
Write each string's length, then a '#' to mark where the number ends, then the raw string: "4#hire". To decode, read the digits up to the next '#', then copy exactly that many characters.

approaches.name: Join with a delimiter
approaches.idea: strs.join(',') and split(','). Wrong: ["a,b"] and ["a", "b"] both become "a,b", and [] and [""] both become "". No choice of delimiter fixes it when strings may contain any character.

approaches.name: Delimiter with escaping
approaches.idea: Escape special characters inside each string (like CSV quoting, or a backslash before every '#' and '\'), then join with '#'. Correct, but the decoder must parse escapes character by character and the edge cases are easy to get wrong.

approaches.name: Length prefix ("4#word")
approaches.idea: Write length + '#' + string for each string. The decoder reads the number up to the next '#' and slices exactly that many characters, so no character is special inside a string.

solution.summary: I prefix every string with its length and a '#': ["hire", "ready"] becomes "4#hire5#ready". To decode, I read the digits up to the next '#', turn them into a length, copy exactly that many characters and jump past them. The decoder never searches inside a string, so any character — even '#' or digits — is safe. Both directions are O(N) in the total length.
solution.explanation:
**Why a plain delimiter fails.** Joining with `','` maps two different lists to the same string: `["a,b"]` and `["a", "b"]` both become `"a,b"`. Once two inputs share an encoding, *no* decoder can get both right. Picking a rarer delimiter only hides the bug, because the strings may contain any character. It also cannot tell `[]` from `[""]`: both join to `""`.

**Length-prefix format.** For each string write `length + '#' + string`:

`["a#", "12", ""]` → `"2#a#"` + `"2#12"` + `"0#"` = `"2#a#2#120#"`

**Decoding** with an index `i` that always points at the start of a length:
1. `j` = position of the first `'#'` at or after `i`. Only digits sit between `i` and `j`, so this `'#'` really is the separator.
2. `length = Number(encoded.slice(i, j))`.
3. The string is the next `length` characters: `encoded.slice(j + 1, j + 1 + length)`.
4. Jump: `i = j + 1 + length`, and repeat until `i` reaches the end.

**Why it is correct.** The decoder only *searches* for `'#'` inside a length header, which contains nothing but digits. Inside a string it *counts* instead of searching, so a `'#'` or digits there are copied blindly. Multi-digit lengths such as `12#` work because all digits up to the `'#'` are read.

**Cost.** Every character is written once and read once: O(N) time and O(N) space, where N is the total length of all strings plus a few header characters per string. Build the output with `StringBuilder` in Java and `"".join(...)` in Python. In JavaScript `+=` is fine in practice: V8, the engine in Node.js and Chrome, stores a concatenation as a rope (a *cons string*) and copies the characters only when the string is first read. `parts.join('')` works too.

**Real-world version.** Length-prefixed framing is how many protocols split a stream into messages: Redis's RESP protocol sends a bulk string as `$5\r\nhello\r\n`, and every HTTP/2 frame starts with a 24-bit length field.

code.code:
def encode(strs: list[str]) -> str:
    return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)  # "4#word"


def decode(encoded: str) -> list[str]:
    result = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(encoded):
        j = encoded.index("#", i)  # the first '#' after i ends the length
        length = int(encoded[i:j])
        result.append(encoded[j + 1 : j + 1 + length])  # exactly length chars
        i = j + 1 + length  # jump past the string, even if it contains '#'
    return result

complexity.time: O(N) — N = total characters; each one is written once by encode and read once by decode
complexity.space: O(N) — the encoded string and the decoded list (headers add only a few characters per string)

keyPoints: A plain delimiter is ambiguous: ["a,b"] and ["a", "b"] encode to the same string
Length prefix + separator ("4#hire"): the '#' only ends the number
The decoder counts characters instead of searching, so '#' and digits inside strings are safe
Lengths can have several digits: read all digits up to the '#'
O(N) time and space; use StringBuilder / join instead of repeated string copies
Same idea as length-prefixed network protocols (Redis RESP, HTTP/2 frames)

visuals.title: Length-prefix encode and decode of ["a#", "12", ""]
visuals.caption: Orange = a length header, blue/green = string payloads, grey = finished headers. The decoder searches for '#' only inside headers and copies payloads by count.

steps.note: Encode `s = "a#"`: write its length 2, a `'#'`, then the raw text. The `'#'` inside "a#" is copied as-is — it does not need escaping. `out = "2#a#"`.
`s = "12"`: append "2#12". Digits inside a string are fine too, because the decoder will know the length before it reaches them. `out = "2#a#2#12"`.
`s = ""`: append "0#" — the empty string still gets a header, so it is not lost. Final `out = "2#a#2#120#"` (10 characters).
Decode. `i = 0` is the start of a length. `indexOf('#', i)` finds `j = 1`, so the length is `encoded.slice(0, 1)` = "2" → 2.
Copy exactly 2 characters after `j`: `slice(2, 4)` = "a#". The `'#'` at index 3 is just data — we count characters, we never search inside the string. Then `i = j + 1 + length = 4`.
`i = 4`. The search starts **after** "a#", so its `'#'` is never mistaken for a separator. `j = 5` → length 2.
Copy 2 characters: "12". The digits 1 and 2 are not read as a length, because the decoder already knows this string is 2 characters long. `i = 8`.
`i = 8`, `j = 9` → length 0. A length of 0 is perfectly valid.
Copy 0 characters: `slice(10, 10)` = "" — the empty string is restored. `i = 10`.
`i = 10` equals `encoded.length`, so the loop stops and `decode` returns ["a#", "12", ""] — exactly the input, including the `'#'`, the digits and the empty string.

visuals.title: Why a plain delimiter cannot work
visuals.caption: Two different lists that join to the same string can never both be decoded correctly.

steps.note: `["a,b"].join(',')` is "a,b". The comma at index 1 is **part of the string**, but nothing in the output says so.
`["a", "b"].join(',')` is **also** "a,b" — here the comma is a separator. Two different inputs, one identical encoding.

The decoder receives the same "a,b" both times, so it must return the same list. `split(',')` gives ["a", "b"], which is wrong for ["a,b"]. A rarer delimiter only hides the bug, because a string may contain any character; [] and [""] also both join to "".
Length prefix: "3#a,b" vs "1#a1#b". The encodings now differ, and the comma inside "a,b" is simply one of the 3 counted characters, so each encoding decodes back to its own list.

pitfalls: Reading only one digit for the length, which breaks for strings of 10 or more characters
Splitting the whole encoded string on '#', which brings the delimiter bug back
Searching for the next '#' from the start of the payload instead of jumping to i = j + 1 + length
Encoding [] and [""] the same way (both as "")

followUps.question: What if the strings contain emoji or Bangla text?
followUps.answer: It still round-trips as long as encode and decode measure length the same way (JavaScript and Java count UTF-16 code units, Python counts code points). If the encoded text is sent as bytes to a service in another language, prefix the UTF-8 byte length instead.

followUps.question: Can you avoid the '#' separator?
followUps.answer: Use a fixed-width length, e.g. always 4 characters ("0004hire") or 4 raw bytes. The decoder reads exactly 4 characters for the length, then the payload: no searching at all, at the cost of a few extra bytes per string.

followUps.question: Where is this used in real systems?
followUps.answer: Anywhere a byte stream must be split into messages: Redis RESP bulk strings ($5\r\nhello\r\n), Protocol Buffers' length-delimited fields and HTTP/2 frames all put the length before the data.

questions.title: Rotate Image (Rotate a Matrix 90°)
questions.prompt:
A square image is stored as an `n × n` matrix of pixel values. Turn it **90 degrees clockwise, in place**: change `matrix` itself instead of building a second n × n matrix.

After the rotation, the first row is the old first column read from bottom to top.

examples.explanation: The old first column 1, 4, 7 read bottom-up becomes the first row 7, 4, 1.
Each corner moves one corner clockwise: 1 to the top-right, 4 to the bottom-right, 16 to the bottom-left, 13 to the top-left. Every other cell turns the same way.
A 1 × 1 matrix is unchanged.

hints: Write down where the cell at (r, c) ends up. Try a few cells of the 3 × 3 example.
(r, c) moves to (c, n − 1 − r). Can you reach that with two simpler moves that are each easy to do in place?
Transpose (swap matrix[r][c] and matrix[c][r] for c > r), then reverse every row.

approaches.name: Copy into a new matrix
approaches.idea: result[c][n − 1 − r] = matrix[r][c] for every cell, then copy back. Simple, but uses O(n²) extra space, which the problem forbids.

approaches.name: Rotate ring by ring (4-way swap)
approaches.idea: For each ring, move four cells at a time with one temp variable: top → right → bottom → left → top. In place, but the index arithmetic is easy to get wrong.

approaches.name: Transpose, then reverse each row
approaches.idea: Mirror across the main diagonal, then mirror left-right. Two short loops, each easy to get right.

solution.summary: A 90° clockwise turn sends (r, c) to (c, n − 1 − r). I get there in place in two easy steps: transpose the matrix (swap matrix[r][c] and matrix[c][r] above the diagonal), then reverse every row. That is O(n²) time, which is optimal because every cell except the centre of an odd-sized matrix has to move, and O(1) extra space.
solution.explanation:
**Where does each cell go?** In a clockwise turn the old first column becomes the first row (read bottom-up), so the cell at row r, column c lands at row c, column n − 1 − r:

`(r, c) → (c, n − 1 − r)`

**Split it into two moves that are easy in place.**
1. **Transpose** — mirror across the main diagonal: `(r, c) → (c, r)`. Swap `matrix[r][c]` with `matrix[c][r]` only for `c > r`; visiting every pair would swap each pair twice and undo the work. Diagonal cells stay put.
2. **Reverse each row** — mirror left-right: `(c, r) → (c, n − 1 − r)`.

Doing both gives exactly `(r, c) → (c, n − 1 − r)`, the clockwise rotation.

**Complexity.** The transpose does n(n − 1)/2 swaps and the reversals do n · ⌊n/2⌋ swaps: O(n²) time. You cannot do better, since every cell except the centre of an odd-sized matrix has to move. Extra space is one temporary per swap: O(1).

**Other rotations from the same building blocks**
- 90° counter-clockwise: transpose, then reverse each **column** (or reverse each row first, then transpose).
- 180°: reverse the order of the rows, then reverse each row.

**Edge cases.** n = 1 (nothing moves), odd n (the centre cell stays where it is). Values do not matter at all — we only move cells.

complexity.time: O(n²) — n(n − 1)/2 transpose swaps plus n · ⌊n/2⌋ reversal swaps; optimal, since every cell except the centre of an odd n moves
complexity.space: O(1) — only a temporary for each swap

keyPoints: Mapping: (r, c) → (c, n − 1 − r)
Transpose (swap only above the diagonal, c > r), then reverse each row
O(n²) time — optimal, (almost) every cell must move; O(1) extra space
Counter-clockwise = transpose + reverse each column; 180° = reverse the rows + reverse each row
Mention the ring-by-ring 4-way swap as the other in-place method

visuals.title: Transpose, then reverse each row (4 × 4)
visuals.caption: Phase 1: blue = the pair being swapped, light blue = already swapped. Phase 2: blue = the row being reversed, light blue = rows still to reverse, green = finished rows.

steps.note: n = 4. Goal: the cell at (r, c) must end at (c, n − 1 − r) — e.g. 13 at (3, 0) must end at (0, 0). Phase 1 is the **transpose**: mirror across the main diagonal 1, 6, 11, 16, which stays in place.
r = 0, c = 1: swap `matrix[0][1]` (2) with `matrix[1][0]` (5). Only cells with c > r are visited — swapping every pair would swap each one twice and undo the work.
r = 0, c = 2: swap `matrix[0][2]` (3) with `matrix[2][0]` (9).
r = 0, c = 3: swap `matrix[0][3]` (4) with `matrix[3][0]` (13).
r = 1, c = 2: swap `matrix[1][2]` (7) with `matrix[2][1]` (10).
r = 1, c = 3: swap `matrix[1][3]` (8) with `matrix[3][1]` (14).
r = 2, c = 3: swap `matrix[2][3]` (12) with `matrix[3][2]` (15). **Transpose done:** row r now holds what was column r.

Phase 2, reverse row 0: [1, 5, 9, 13] → [13, 9, 5, 1]. Mirroring left-right moves column x to column n − 1 − x, so a value that the transpose put at (c, r) lands at (c, n − 1 − r) — its clockwise position.

Phase 2, reverse row 1: [2, 6, 10, 14] → [14, 10, 6, 2]. Mirroring left-right moves column x to column n − 1 − x, so a value that the transpose put at (c, r) lands at (c, n − 1 − r) — its clockwise position.

Phase 2, reverse row 2: [3, 7, 11, 15] → [15, 11, 7, 3]. Mirroring left-right moves column x to column n − 1 − x, so a value that the transpose put at (c, r) lands at (c, n − 1 − r) — its clockwise position.
Reverse row 3: [4, 8, 12, 16] → [16, 12, 8, 4]. **Done.** The old first column 1, 5, 9, 13 read bottom-up is now the first row 13, 9, 5, 1 — a 90° clockwise turn, using only swaps.

visuals.title: Every square rotation from two building blocks
visuals.caption: All recipes were checked against the index mapping. "Reverse each column" = swap row i with row n − 1 − i.
rows: Transpose, then reverse each column (or reverse each row, then transpose)
Reverse the order of the rows, then reverse each row
Swap matrix[r][c] and matrix[c][r] for c > r

pitfalls: Starting the inner transpose loop at c = 0 instead of r + 1: every pair is swapped twice, so the transpose undoes itself and the result is only mirrored left-right
Reversing the columns instead of the rows, which turns the matrix counter-clockwise
Building a new matrix and reassigning the local variable (matrix = result): the caller still sees the old matrix
Trying the same trick in place on a non-square m × n matrix — the result is n × m, so it needs a new matrix

followUps.question: How would you rotate counter-clockwise?
followUps.answer: Transpose, then reverse each column (swap row i with row n − 1 − i). Equivalently: reverse each row first, then transpose.

followUps.question: What about a non-square m × n matrix?
followUps.answer: The result is n × m, so it cannot live in the same array: allocate result with n rows and m columns and set result[c][m − 1 − r] = matrix[r][c]. In-place only works for squares.

followUps.question: Can each cell move only once?
followUps.answer: Yes, rotate ring by ring: for each ring and offset, cycle four cells with one temp (the top value goes to the right side, right to bottom, bottom to left, left to top). Same O(n²), but harder to get right in an interview.

questions.title: Spiral Matrix
questions.prompt:
List the elements of a matrix with `m` rows and `n` columns in **spiral order**: start at the top-left corner, go right along the top row, down the right column, left along the bottom row, up the left column, and keep spiralling inwards until every element has been visited exactly once. Return them as one list.

The matrix does **not** have to be square.

examples.explanation: After the outer ring only the middle row 7, 8, 9 is left; it is read once, left to right.
A single column: the top row gives 1, the right column gives 2 and 3, and nothing is left.

hints: Peel the matrix like an onion: read the outer ring, then the ring inside it.
Keep four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right. After reading the top row do top++, after the right column right--, and so on.
With a non-square matrix the last ring can be a single row or column. Check top <= bottom before the bottom-row pass and left <= right before the left-column pass, or you read it twice.

approaches.name: Simulate with a visited matrix
approaches.idea: Walk with a direction (right, down, left, up) and turn clockwise when the next cell is outside the matrix or already visited. Easy to reason about, but needs an m × n visited array (or overwriting the input).

approaches.name: Shrinking boundaries
approaches.idea: Track top, bottom, left and right. Read the top row, right column, bottom row and left column of the current ring, shrinking a boundary after each side, and guard the last two sides for single-row or single-column rings.

solution.summary: I keep four boundaries — top, bottom, left, right — and peel the matrix ring by ring: the top row left to right then top++, the right column downwards then right--, then the bottom row right to left and the left column upwards, each guarded so a single leftover row or column is not read twice. Every element is read once: O(m·n) time and O(1) extra space besides the output.
solution.explanation:
**Picture it as peeling rings.** The outer ring is the top row, the right column, the bottom row (backwards) and the left column (upwards). Then the same thing repeats on the smaller matrix inside.

**Four boundaries** describe the part that is still unread: rows `top..bottom` and columns `left..right`, all inclusive. While both ranges are non-empty:
1. **→ Top row:** columns `left..right` of row `top`, then `top++`.
2. **↓ Right column:** rows `top..bottom` of column `right`, then `right--`.
3. **← Bottom row:** only if `top <= bottom` — columns `right..left` of row `bottom`, then `bottom--`.
4. **↑ Left column:** only if `left <= right` — rows `bottom..top` of column `left`, then `left++`.

**Why the two guards?** Steps 1 and 2 shrink the boundaries, so by step 3 the rectangle may already be empty. In a 3 × 5 matrix the inner ring is the single row `7 8 9`: step 1 reads it and moves `top` below `bottom`. Without the guard, step 3 would walk the same row backwards and add 8 and 7 again. A single leftover **column** causes the same problem in step 4. In a square matrix the last ring is a full ring or a single cell, and there the unguarded passes happen to read nothing — which is why this bug survives a 3 × 3 test. Always try 1 × n, n × 1 and a wide or tall matrix.

**Complexity.** Each element is pushed exactly once: O(m·n) time. Apart from the output list we keep four integers: O(1) extra space.

code.code:
def spiral_order(matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    result = []
    top, bottom = 0, len(matrix) - 1
    left, right = 0, len(matrix[0]) - 1
    while top <= bottom and left <= right:
        for c in range(left, right + 1):  # → top row
            result.append(matrix[top][c])
        top += 1
        for r in range(top, bottom + 1):  # ↓ right column
            result.append(matrix[r][right])
        right -= 1
        if top <= bottom:  # a row is still unread: ← bottom row
            for c in range(right, left - 1, -1):
                result.append(matrix[bottom][c])
            bottom -= 1
        if left <= right:  # a column is still unread: ↑ left column
            for r in range(bottom, top - 1, -1):
                result.append(matrix[r][left])
            left += 1
    return result

complexity.time: O(m·n) — every element is pushed exactly once
complexity.space: O(1) extra — four boundary variables (the output list is not counted)

keyPoints: Four inclusive boundaries top/bottom/left/right; shrink one after each side
Order: → top row, ↓ right column, ← bottom row, ↑ left column
Guard the bottom-row pass with top <= bottom and the left-column pass with left <= right
Test non-square shapes (1 × n, n × 1, 3 × 5): squares hide the bug
O(m·n) time, O(1) extra space

visuals.caption: Blue = cells read by the current pass, light blue = already in result, red = cells the guard stops us from reading twice.

steps.note: Four boundaries describe the unread part: rows `top..bottom` = 0..2 and columns `left..right` = 0..4. Each ring is read → along the top row, ↓ down the right column, ← along the bottom row, ↑ up the left column.
→ Top row: columns 0..4 of row 0 give 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. That row is finished, so `top++` → 1.
↓ Right column: rows 1..2 of column 4 give 10, 15. It starts at the new `top`, so 5 is not read twice. `right--` → 3.
`top` (1) ≤ `bottom` (2), so a row is still unread. ← Bottom row from column 3 down to 0: 14, 13, 12, 11. `bottom--` → 1.
`left` (0) ≤ `right` (3). ↑ Left column from row 1 up to row 1: 6. `left++` → 1. The outer ring is done.
top = bottom = 1 and left..right = 1..3: the inner "ring" is a **single row**. → Top row reads 7, 8, 9; `top++` → 2, which is now **below** `bottom` (1).
↓ Right column: the loop runs from r = 2 to 1, so it reads nothing. `right--` → 2.

Guard: `top` (2) > `bottom` (1), so the bottom-row pass is **skipped**. Without this check it would walk row 1 backwards and add 8 and 7 a second time — the classic bug that only non-square matrices expose.
`left` (1) ≤ `right` (2), but the ↑ pass runs from r = 1 up to r = 2, so it reads nothing; `left++` → 2. Now `top` > `bottom`, the while loop ends and all 15 elements were read exactly once.
