pitfalls: Leaving out the two guards, so a single leftover row or column is read twice
Assuming the matrix is square and using one size n for both dimensions
Changing a boundary before the pass that still needs it, e.g. right-- before walking the right column
Off-by-one loop bounds: the boundaries are inclusive, so the loops use <= and >=

followUps.question: How would you fill an n × n matrix with 1..n² in spiral order?
followUps.answer: Use the same boundary loop, but write counter++ into each cell instead of reading it (often called Spiral Matrix II).

followUps.question: How would you go counter-clockwise from the top-left?
followUps.answer: Change the order of the passes: ↓ left column, → bottom row, ↑ right column, ← top row, with the same shrink-and-guard logic.

questions.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
questions.prompt:
You get an `m × n` matrix of integers. Every cell that holds `0` wipes out its **whole row and whole column**: all of those cells must become `0`. Change `matrix` **in place** and return nothing.

Only the zeros that are in the matrix **at the start** count: zeros you write must not spread further. Aim for O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: The zero at (1, 2) clears row 1 and column 2; the zero at (3, 0) clears row 3 and column 0.
Only row 0 and column 1 are cleared. The zeros written into row 0 must not clear columns 0 and 2.
A zero in the corner clears row 0 and column 0.

constraints: -2³¹ ≤ matrix[i][j] ≤ 2³¹ − 1 (any int, so no value is free to use as a special marker)
hints: If you clear a row and column the moment you find a 0, the zeros you write look exactly like original zeros. Record first, clear second.
Two boolean arrays (one per row, one per column) give O(m + n) extra space. Where inside the matrix could you keep those flags instead?
Use row 0 as the column flags and column 0 as the row flags. matrix[0][0] can only serve one of them, so keep one extra boolean for column 0 — and clear row 0 and column 0 last.

approaches.name: Copy the matrix
approaches.idea: For every 0 in a copy, clear its row and column in the original. Correct, but O(m·n) extra space and slow when there are many zeros.

approaches.name: Row and column flag arrays
approaches.idea: Pass 1 sets zeroRow[r] and zeroCol[c] for every 0. Pass 2 clears cell (r, c) if zeroRow[r] or zeroCol[c].

approaches.name: Markers in row 0 and column 0 + one flag
approaches.idea: Store zeroCol[c] in matrix[0][c] and zeroRow[r] in matrix[r][0]. matrix[0][0] marks row 0 and a boolean marks column 0. Clear the inner cells first, then row 0, then column 0.

solution.summary: First record which rows and columns must be cleared, then clear them — never both at once, or the zeros I write would spread. For O(1) extra space I keep that record inside the matrix: matrix[r][0] = 0 marks row r and matrix[0][c] = 0 marks column c, plus one boolean for column 0, because matrix[0][0] already marks row 0. Then I clear the inner cells from the markers and finish with row 0 and column 0. O(m·n) time.
solution.explanation:
**Why you cannot clear as you go.** If the scan clears row r and column c the moment it meets a 0, it later meets the zeros it wrote and clears even more, until the whole matrix can be wiped (see the second visual). Original zeros and written zeros must be kept apart, so **record first, clear second**.

**O(m + n) version.** Two boolean arrays, `zeroRow[r]` and `zeroCol[c]`. Pass 1 sets them; pass 2 clears cell (r, c) if `zeroRow[r] || zeroCol[c]`. Explain this one first — it is the clean idea.

**O(1) version: reuse row 0 and column 0 as those arrays.**
- `matrix[0][c]` plays `zeroCol[c]` and `matrix[r][0]` plays `zeroRow[r]`.
- `matrix[0][0]` would have to be both `zeroRow[0]` and `zeroCol[0]`. It keeps the row-0 job, and a separate boolean `firstColZero` remembers whether column 0 itself had a 0.

**The order of the passes matters.**
1. **Pass 1** — for each row r: if `matrix[r][0] === 0`, set `firstColZero`; for every zero at (r, c) with c ≥ 1, write `matrix[r][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][c] = 0`. Overwriting those cells is safe because their row or column is going to be cleared anyway.
2. **Pass 2** — clear every inner cell (r ≥ 1, c ≥ 1) whose row marker or column marker is 0. Row 0 and column 0 still hold the markers, so they can be read.
3. **Pass 3** — if `matrix[0][0] === 0`, clear row 0; then, if `firstColZero`, clear column 0. Clearing row 0 or column 0 before pass 2 would turn every marker in it into 0 and wipe every column (or row), and clearing column 0 before checking `matrix[0][0]` would make row 0 look marked.

**Complexity.** Three passes over the matrix: O(m·n) time. Extra space: one boolean, O(1).

**Edge cases.** 1 × n and m × 1 matrices (one of the inner loops never runs), a 0 at (0, 0), all zeros, no zeros at all.

complexity.time: O(m·n) — three passes over the matrix
complexity.space: O(1) — the markers live in row 0 and column 0; only one extra boolean

keyPoints: Record first, clear second — zeros you write must not spread
O(m + n): two boolean arrays for rows and columns
O(1): keep the flags in row 0 and column 0; matrix[0][0] marks row 0, one boolean marks column 0
Clear the inner cells first, then row 0, then column 0
Do not use a special value like -1 as a marker: any int can appear in the input

visuals.title: O(1)-space markers on a 4 × 5 matrix
visuals.caption: Red = original zeros, orange = markers in row 0 / column 0, blue = the current row or the cells changed in this step, light blue = cleared earlier.

steps.note: Two zeros (red): (1, 2) and (3, 0). We must not clear anything yet — first **record** which rows and columns must become zero, using row 0 and column 0 as the record. `firstColZero` starts as `false`.
Pass 1, r = 0: `matrix[0][0]` is 1, not 0, and columns 1..4 hold no zero, so nothing is recorded.
r = 1: `matrix[1][2]` is 0. Write the markers: `matrix[1][0] = 0` ("clear row 1") and `matrix[0][2] = 0` ("clear column 2"). Overwriting 6 and 3 is safe — those cells are going to be zero anyway.
r = 2: no zeros, nothing to record.

r = 3: `matrix[3][0]` is 0, so column 0 must be cleared → `firstColZero = true`. We cannot record that in `matrix[0][0]`: that cell is row 0's marker, and a 0 there would wrongly clear row 0. The 0 itself already marks row 3.
Pass 2, r = 1: the row marker `matrix[1][0]` is 0, so every inner cell of row 1 becomes 0.
r = 2: the row marker `matrix[2][0]` is 2 (not marked), but the column marker `matrix[0][2]` is 0 → only `matrix[2][2]` becomes 0. The rest of row 2 survives.
r = 3: the row marker `matrix[3][0]` is 0 (the original zero doubles as its marker) → the inner cells of row 3 become 0.
`matrix[0][0]` is 1, so row 0 had no zero of its own and is **not** cleared. Its cell (0, 2) is already 0, which is correct because column 2 must be zero anyway.
`firstColZero` is true, so clear column 0 last: (0, 0) and (2, 0) become 0. Doing this before the `matrix[0][0]` check would have made row 0 look marked.
Done: rows 1 and 3 and columns 0 and 2 are zero, and the 6 other cells keep their values. Three passes over the matrix — O(m·n) time — and the only extra memory was one boolean.

visuals.title: The bug: clearing while you scan
visuals.caption: Red = the real zero, orange = a zero we wrote ourselves being mistaken for a real one, blue = cells cleared in this step.

steps.note: One zero at (0, 1). The correct answer clears only row 0 and column 1. Watch what happens if we clear rows and columns **as soon as the scan sees a 0**.
(0, 1) is a real zero: clear row 0 and column 1. So far this matches the correct answer.
(0, 2) is now 0 — but **we** wrote that zero. The scan cannot tell it from a real one, so it clears column 2 too. Wrong from here on.
(0, 3) is another zero we wrote, so column 3 is cleared as well. The zeros keep cascading.
(1, 1) is another zero we wrote, so row 1 is cleared as well. The zeros keep cascading.
(2, 1) is another zero we wrote, so row 2 is cleared as well. The zeros keep cascading.
Result: the whole matrix is 0, but the correct answer (shown here) keeps 1s in columns 0, 2 and 3 of rows 1 and 2. That is why every correct solution **records first and clears second**.

pitfalls: Clearing rows and columns during the first scan, so the written zeros cascade
Using matrix[0][0] for both row 0 and column 0: a zero in column 0 then wipes row 0 too
Clearing row 0 or column 0 before the inner cells, which destroys the markers
Marking cells with a special value such as -1: any int can be in the matrix, so the marker collides with real data

followUps.question: Why not mark cells with a special value like -1 or null?
followUps.answer: Any int can be in the matrix, so a marker value can collide with real data, and a Java int[][] cannot hold null. The row-0/column-0 markers cannot collide with anything.

followUps.question: Which version would you ship in production code?
followUps.answer: Usually the O(m + n) version with two boolean arrays: it is simpler and has no ordering traps, and m + n booleans are cheap. Give it first in the interview, then optimise to O(1) if asked.

quiz.question: What are the time and space complexity of the one-pass hash map solution to Two Sum?
options: O(n²) time, O(1) space
O(n log n) time, O(1) space
O(n) time, O(n) space
O(n) time, O(1) space
quiz.explanation: One pass with O(1) average lookups gives O(n) time; the map may store every element, so O(n) space. O(n) time with O(1) space needs the array to be sorted already (two pointers).

quiz.question: In Subarray Sum Equals K, why is the map initialised with {0: 1}?
options: To avoid dividing by zero
So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
Because k can never be 0
To make the first lookup faster
quiz.explanation: A subarray nums[0..i] has sum prefix[i]. It is counted when prefix[i] − k = 0 is in the map, which requires the empty prefix (sum 0) to be recorded once before the scan.

quiz.question: Why does a sliding window not solve Subarray Sum Equals K in general?
options: It needs O(n²) memory
It cannot count overlapping subarrays
Sliding windows only work on strings
With negative numbers, growing the window can decrease the sum, so there is no rule for when to shrink
quiz.explanation: A window relies on monotonicity: extending increases the sum, shrinking decreases it. Negative values break that. For all-positive arrays a window does work.

quiz.question: What does this return?
quiz.explanation: The subarray must be non-empty, so the best is the single largest element, −1. Initialising with 0 instead of nums[0] would wrongly return 0.

quiz.question: Which key lets you group anagrams in O(k) per word of length k (lowercase letters)?
options: The word with its letters sorted
The sum of its character codes
Its 26 letter counts joined with a separator
Its first and last letters
quiz.explanation: Counting letters is O(k). Sorting is O(k log k) — correct, but not O(k). The sum is not unique ("ad" and "bc" both sum to 197).

quiz.question: What is the default load factor of Java's HashMap, after which it resizes?
quiz.explanation: Load factor = entries ÷ buckets. Java resizes (doubles the table and rehashes) when it exceeds 0.75 — a balance between memory use and short chains.

quiz.question: What does this print?

code.code:
const s = new Set([1, '1', 1, NaN, NaN]);
console.log(s.size);

quiz.explanation: Set uses SameValueZero: 1 and '1' are different values, the second 1 is a duplicate, and NaN is treated as equal to NaN. So the set holds 1, '1' and NaN.

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: TypeError
quiz.explanation: Plain object keys are converted to strings: 1 and "1" are the same key "1" (overwritten), true becomes "true". Two keys. Use a Map when keys are not strings.

quiz.question: Longest Consecutive Sequence uses a while loop inside a for loop. Why is it still O(n)?
options: The while loop only runs from run starts, so across the whole algorithm it extends over each number at most once
Set lookups make while loops O(1)
The array is sorted first
It is not; it is O(n²)
quiz.explanation: Because x − 1 must be missing before counting starts, each run is walked exactly once from its smallest number. The total work of all while loops is at most n.

quiz.question: How does Product of Array Except Self achieve O(1) extra space (not counting the output)?
options: Divide the total product by nums[i]
Sort the array first
Use a hash map from index to product
Write prefix products into the output array, then multiply in a running suffix product from the right
quiz.explanation: The output array doubles as the prefix array, and the suffix is a single variable. Division is banned and fails with zeros.

quiz.question: In open addressing with linear probing, why is a deleted slot marked with a tombstone instead of being emptied?
options: To save memory
An emptied slot would end later probe sequences early, so keys stored past it would be reported missing
Tombstones make inserts O(1) in the worst case
Arrays cannot contain empty slots
quiz.explanation: Lookups stop at the first empty slot. If a slot in the middle of a probe path were emptied, any key placed after it on that path would become unreachable.

quiz.question: In Java, a class overrides equals() but not hashCode() and is used as a HashMap key. What can happen?
options: get() with an equal but different object can return null, because the two objects have different hash codes
Nothing — HashMap only calls equals()
The code does not compile
put() throws an exception
quiz.explanation: HashMap first uses hashCode() to pick the bucket. The default hashCode is identity-based, so an equal object usually goes to a different bucket and equals() is never even called.
